name: Ocaina
confidence_why: Agnew and Pike 1957, the only published phonology of Ocaina, describe two contrastive pitch levels with high-low-low and low-high-low both possible in three-syllable words, and Leach 1969/2008 and Fagua and Seifart 2010 independently mark the same high-pitched syllables with an acute "acento" without offering a competing analysis, so the tonal-or-pitch accent coding rests on few but agreeing first-hand sources that differ only in whether they call the prominence tone or accent.
catalog_citation: Agnew, Arlene & Evelyn G. Pike. 1957. Phonemes of Ocaina (Huitoto). International Journal of American Linguistics 23(1): 24-27. doi:10.1086/464385. Open scan: Rosetta Project, archive.org
catalog_quote: 3. There is contrastive pitch in Ocaina as seen in the following words (the acute accent over a vowel indicates high tone, whereas a vowel without such an accent indicates low tone): /xóótʸo/ your game bird; /xootʸo/ game bird; /tʸáxotʸo/ I sell it; /tʸaxotʸó/ I need to sell it; /ñonǫ́ǫ́ha/ kind of pod; /ñonǫǫha/ wood worms. The following tone groups illustrate the two contrastive tone levels. In two syllable words there is contrast between high-low and low-low as illustrated by two samples from each group: /tóto óxï/ big grandmother; ... /koño óxï/ big bird; ... In three syllable words there is contrast between low-low-low; low-high-low and high-low-low: /dʸaraga óxï/ a big cut tree; /porótʸa óxï/ big bean; /kážoho óxï/ big parrot. Low tone is optionally progressively lower in pitch from the beginning to the end of the utterance. ... Low tones are much more frequent in occurrence than high tones. Tone is involved in the morphophonemics of the language: maaxa ~ mááxa- ~ maaxá- walk ... Tone also frequently indicates items such as mode, tense, person, etc. as: ihï óxï hóórorï he must crawl like an animal a lot; ihï óxï hoorórï he is going to crawl like an animal a lot; pïïxo axe; píïxo your axe.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (4 pp., Rosetta Project scan, archive.org rosettaproject_oca_phon-1; the PDF's metadata gives the title 'Ocaina Phonology'). Rendered PDF pages 2-3 (= IJAL XXIII pp. 25-26) and read the page scan. Section '3.' begins at the foot of p. 25 col. 2 ('3. There is contrastive pitch in Ocaina') and continues on p. 26 col. 1: '(the acute accent over a vowel indicates high tone, whereas a vowel without such an accent indicates low tone): /xóótʸo/ your game bird; /xootʸo/ game bird; /tʸáxotʸo/ I sell it; /tʸaxotʸó/ I need to sell it; /ñonóóha/ kind of pod; /ñonooha/ wood worms. The following tone groups illustrate the two contrastive tone levels. In two syllable words there is contrast between…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ocaina is described as a two-level tone language (high vs. low on each vowel/mora); the position of high tone is lexically and morphologically determined (any syllable, more than one syllable may be high, e.g. /xóótʸo/, /tʸaxotʸó/), and the article says nothing about stress. The complementary statement in Leach 1969 (Vocabulario ocaina p. 163) treats the same prominence as an accent: the written acute marks 'la sílaba o sílabas que llevan la mayor fuerza de voz', read at relatively high pitch; words with no accent are read low 'con acento menguante en la primera sílaba' (foojo 'la casa' vs fóójo 'tu casa'). So on both accounts the prominent syllable is lexically placed (unpredictable) and realized as high pitch, not positionally fixed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned by Agnew & Pike. Leach 1969 p. 163 notes only that words with no written accent are read with a low tone and a 'diminishing accent' on the first syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Tone/accent is morphophonemic: it varies within paradigms (maaxa ~ mááxa- ~ maaxá- 'walk'), marks mode, tense and person (piixo 'axe' vs pïïxo 'your axe'), and accent shift forms plurals (Leach 1969 p. ~167; Fagua & Seifart 2010 p. 228) and some oblique case marking (Fagua & Seifart 2010 p. 234). Low tone downdrifts progressively through the utterance.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: tone contrasts are given on isolated words and on words inside short phrases (e.g.. óxï 'a lot'); Leach's statement concerns citation forms in a bilingual dictionary. Agnew & Pike's data: Peruvian Ocaina (Yaguasyacu, Ampiyacu, Algodón, Putumayo rivers, collected 1955-56); Leach: 'dialecto uvohsa' (speakers from La Chorrera, Colombia and Puerto Isango, Peru).
new_statements.identity_note: Both open primary sources describe Peruvian/Uvohsa Ocaina: Agnew & Pike 1957 (data from the Yaguasyacu, Ampiyacu, Algodón and Putumayo rivers, NE Peru, 1955-56) and Leach 1969/2008 ('dialecto uvohsa', consultants from La Chorrera, Colombia, and Puerto Isango, Peru). Glottolog 5.1 lists no dialect nodes under ocai1244, so no separate glottocode applies; Fagua 2004/2013 also treat the uvohsa variety.

new_statements.quote: p. 163: "El acento ortográfico ocaina se semeja al castellano, indicando la sílaba o sílabas que llevan la mayor fuerza de voz. Se lee la sílaba que lleva el acento ortográfico en tono relativamente elevado a las sílabas no acentuadas. Palabras sin acento ortográfico se leen con tono de voz relativamente bajo y con acento menguante en la primera sílaba: foojo la casa, fóójo tu casa." p. 165: "El prefijo que indica \"tu\" es voz alta en la primera sílaba de la raíz o cero cuando la raíz básica tiene voz alta en la primera sílaba." p. 167: "El cambio del acento también es otra manera de formar el plural. Casi todos los nombres, cuando ocurren con los sufijos de descripción, forman el plural así: dyahóóhco raíz gruesa / dyahohcón raíces"
new_statements.translation: p. 163: "The Ocaina orthographic accent resembles the Spanish one, indicating the syllable or syllables that carry the greatest force of voice. The syllable bearing the orthographic accent is read at a tone relatively higher than the unaccented syllables. Words without an orthographic accent are read with a relatively low tone of voice and with a fading accent on the first syllable: foojo 'the house', fóójo 'your house'." p. 165: "The prefix meaning 'your' is high voice on the first syllable of the root, or zero when the basic root already has high voice on the first syllable." p. 167: "Change of accent is also another way of forming the plural. Almost all nouns, when they occur with descriptive suffixes, form the plural thus: dyahóóhco 'thick root' / dyahohcón 'roots'"

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Ocaina has an empty rule and the existing statement (Agnew & Pike 1957) reads the language as tonal (two-level contrastive pitch) with no stress statement. Leach's orthographic note is compatible with that: her 'acento' is realized as relatively high tone, i.e. it is Agnew & Pike's high tone, and her minimal pair foojo/fóójo matches their /xootʸo/ vs /xóótʸo/ 'game bird / your game bird'. It adds a stress-like statement (the accented syllable also carries 'la mayor fuerza de voz'), and shows the accent is lexically contrastive and morphologically mobile (possession, plural). It is a practical-orthography note, not a phonological analysis, so it refines rather than ove…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The accent (written with an acute, Spanish-style) marks the syllable or syllables with the greatest force of voice, which are pronounced at relatively high pitch; unaccented words are read low with a fading prominence on the first syllable. Its position is not predictable from word shape: it is lexically contrastive (foojo 'house' vs fóójo 'your house') and is moved by morphology (2sg possession = high voice on the first root syllable; the plural of nouns with descriptive suffixes shifts the accent to the final syllable, dyahóóhco > dyahohcón). A word may carry more than one accented syllable or none.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed; 'la sílaba o sílabas' allows several accented syllables per word with no hierarchy stated.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated as exceptions; accent shift is itself a grammatical process (plural, possession). Description is of the Uvohsa dialect.
new_statements.identity_note: Leach 2008 describes the Uvohsa (Uvoohsa) dialect of Ocaina, with speakers from La Chorrera (Amazonas, Colombia) and Puerto Isango, Río Yaguasyacu (Peru); Fagua 2013 is also on the Uvoohsa dialect per its subject keywords. Agnew & Pike 1957 (catalog) is the same language, Peruvian data.

tone_statements.quote: Planteamos, por ahora como hipótesis, que el ocaina es una lengua acentual, afirmación que será paulatinamente desarrollada y precisada. [...] El peso silábico corresponde a una realización segmental: oclusión glotal en posición de coda (1) y a dos manifestaciones suprasegmentales: alargamiento vocálico [Vː] (2a) y altura tonal: tono alto [V́] (2b) o contorno tonal ascendente [V̌] (2c). [...] El acento que se manifiesta como altura tonal es en ocaina un rasgo fonológicamente pertinente (4). La elevación tonal es susceptible de asignarse a un segmento o bien ser flotante
tone_statements.translation: We propose, for now as a hypothesis, that Ocaina is an accentual language, a claim that will be progressively developed and refined. [...] Syllable weight corresponds to one segmental realisation, a glottal stop in coda position (1), and to two suprasegmental manifestations: vowel lengthening [Vː] (2a) and tonal height: high tone [V́] (2b) or rising tonal contour [V̌] (2c). [...] The accent that manifests itself as tonal height is a phonologically relevant feature in Ocaina (4). The tonal rise may be assigned to a segment or be floating

readall_conflicts: No direct conflict. Agnew & Pike (1957, already in the catalog) analyse Ocaina prominence as two-level contrastive pitch and never use the word stress; Leach (1969/2008) calls the same high-pitched syllables the 'acento', described as greatest force of voice plus relatively high tone, with a Spanish-style acute. The two descriptions cover the same phenomenon (the minimal pairs match: foojo/fóójo 'house / your house' = Agnew & Pike's /xootʸo/ vs /xóótʸo/), differing only in whether it is labelled tone or accent; Leach's remark that a word can carry several accented syllables or none points to tone rather than a culminative stress. Fagua & Seifart 2010 (held by the project from the earlier reading) state that the published phonology remains Agnew & Pike 1957. Fagua 2013 could not be opened.

sources.note: Sec. 3 'Tone' (pp. 25-26): Ocaina has contrastive pitch with two tone levels (high, marked with acute; low unmarked); 2-syllable words contrast HL vs LL, 3-syllable words LLL, LHL, HLL; low tones far more frequent; tone is morphophonemic and marks mode/tense/person. The word 'stress' never appears; no stress statement. (Full 4-page article via Rosetta Project scan on archive.org; page scan checked.)
